findings.message: For a non-seekable stream with an unbounded DataSpec, `bytesRemaining` is set to `C.LengthUnset` (-1), and the `bytesRemaining < 0` guard then throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Non-seekable streams can never open on Android. MediaSource.FromStream(networkStream or GZipStream) with CanSeek=false: length = C.LengthUnset, dataSpec.Length = C.LengthUnset, so bytesRemaining = -1, Open throws 'Position 0 exceeds stream length -1', and playback fails with a loader error. The guard needs `bytesRemaining < 0 && bytesRemaining != C.LengthUnset`.

FillDataRequest makes one `stream.Read` call and then calls FinishLoading. `Stream.Read` may return fewer bytes than requested, so AVFoundation gets a truncated range. Separately, `(int)RequestedLength` overflows for ranges over 2 GB, and the whole range is buffered three times (byte[], the `buffer[..bytesRead]` slice, and NSData). With a FileStream or BufferedStream, Read returns, say, 81920 bytes out of a 5 MB request. Respond sends the partial data, FinishLoading marks the request complete, and AVFoundation decodes garbage or fails. When RequestsAllDataToEndOfResource asks for a 600 MB file, about 1.8 GB is allocated (OOM on iOS). For anything over 2 GB the int cast goes negative and `new byte[]` throws (silently caught). Read in a loop and respond in chunks.

Exceptions in FillDataRequest are caught and logged, and then `loadingRequest.FinishLoading()` is still called. AVFoundation is told the request succeeded with no data, instead of getting FinishLoadingWithError. The app disposes the stream, or a read throws IOException. The catch logs to Debug, FinishLoading() reports success with zero bytes, and AVFoundation stalls or reports a generic 'cannot open' error. MediaFailed never gets the real cause.

The StreamDataSourceFactory (a Java.Lang.Object) is disposed before the player's media source is replaced: before `await SetPlayerData`, and again inside CreateMediaItemFromStream. ExoPlayer still holds the Java peer and can call createDataSource on a disposed managed peer. iOS has the same pattern: the resource loader is disposed before ReplaceCurrentItemWithPlayerItem. A stream source is playing with ShouldLoopPlayback=true. The user switches to a UriMediaSource that has MetadataArtworkUrl set. The factory is disposed, then the artwork HTTP download is awaited. Meanwhile ExoPlayer creates the next looping period, which calls createDataSource on the released peer: 'Unable to activate instance of type StreamDataSourceFactory' (crash). Dispose the old factory only after SetMediaSource/SetMediaItem has replaced it.

When a StreamMediaSource has a null Stream, SetPlayerData falls through to `return mediaItem` (the stale builder from the previous source). Because the Source is still a StreamMediaSource, the old factory is not disposed, and the old stream is re-prepared through ProgressiveMediaSource. The app sets `streamMediaSource.Stream = null` after disposing its stream to clear playback. PlatformUpdateSource keeps currentStreamDataSourceFactory, builds the stale 'stream://media' item, and calls SetMediaSource. ExoPlayer then reads the disposed stream (ObjectDisposedException, MediaFailed) instead of clearing to None.

For non-seekable streams, the loader reports ContentLength 0 and then serves every data request from the stream's current position, ignoring RequestedOffset. AVFoundation receives bytes that don't match the requested range. AVFoundation probes bytes 0-1, then requests a range near the end (for example the moov atom). A non-seekable stream just returns the next sequential bytes as if they were at that offset, so the asset is corrupt or fails to load. ContentLength=0 also tells AVFoundation the resource is empty.

GetStreamContentType returns 'public.mpeg-4' for every non-ftyp stream, so MP3, WAV, FLAC and similar streams get the wrong UTI. It also re-implements, less completely, the shared StreamExtensions.GetMimeType, which is already compiled for iOS and could be mapped to a UTI. MediaSource.FromStream(mp3Stream) on iOS: the content type is reported as public.mpeg-4, AVFoundation picks the MPEG-4 parser, and the item fails with 'Cannot Open'. Also, the finally block restores Position with no try/catch, so an IOException from Read propagates out of PlatformUpdateSource, unlike the guarded shared helper.

`Stream.AsRandomAccessStream()` throws NotSupportedException when the stream is not seekable. Nothing guards or catches this, so it escapes PlatformUpdateSource. MediaSource.FromStream(await httpClient.GetStreamAsync(url)) on Windows: AsRandomAccessStream throws NotSupportedException from the source-changed path, and the app crashes instead of reporting MediaFailed or falling back.

UpdateSourceStream disposes the MemoryStream the MediaElement is still playing before the new copy finishes. The `sourceStream` field is also assigned and re-read across awaits outside the semaphore, so concurrent callers (OnAppearing plus Open or Record Video) interleave. ReleaseSourceStream also calls WaitAsync inside the try, so a failed wait would still Release. The user taps 'Open Video' while the BuckBunny download from OnAppearing is still copying. Both calls release, both assign `sourceStream`, and the first call's `sourceStream.Position = 0` and FromStream(sourceStream) pick up the other call's half-filled stream. Separately, during any copy the player keeps reading the already disposed old stream, which throws ObjectDisposedException in the native reader.

`httpClient.GetStreamAsync` in the async void OnAppearing is outside UpdateSourceStream's try/catch, so any network failure is an unhandled exception in an async void method. The device is offline, or test-videos.co.uk is unreachable or retries are exhausted. GetStreamAsync throws HttpRequestException, async void rethrows it on the SynchronizationContext, and the sample app crashes as soon as the page opens.

Every StreamDataSource created by the factory seeks and reads the same Stream instance with no locking. ExoPlayer can have more than one period or loader active (looping pre-buffer, seek reload) on different loader threads. With ShouldLoopPlayback, ExoPlayer pre-buffers the next repetition while the current period reloads after a seek. Two loader threads interleave Seek and Read on the same MemoryStream, each gets bytes from the other's offset, and extraction fails or plays corrupted frames.

A first byte of 0x47 alone classifies a stream as MPEG-TS, and the MP3 frame-sync check `(header[1] & 0xE0) == 0xE0` also matches AAC ADTS headers (FF F1/F9), labeling them audio/mpeg. On Windows, an .aac ADTS stream (FF F1 ...) is passed to MediaSource.CreateFromStream as 'audio/mpeg', so the wrong decoder is chosen and playback fails. Any stream starting with 'G' (0x47), such as a GIF, is labeled video/mp2t. Check the layer bits (== 00 means ADTS), and for TS also check for 0x47 at offset 188.

GetMimeType makes one `stream.Read(header)` call. Read may legally return fewer than 16 bytes even when more are available, so detection runs on a truncated header. With a BufferedStream or custom seekable stream whose first Read returns 8 bytes of an MP4, the `header.Length >= 12` ftyp check fails and the result is 'application/octet-stream' (or a wrong match). Use `stream.ReadAtLeast(header, header.Length, throwOnEndOfStream: false)`.

The page is registered as transient and implements IAsyncDisposable. Microsoft.Extensions.DI tracks disposable transients in the resolving (window) scope until that scope is disposed, so every navigation keeps a page instance alive. Each visit to 'MediaElement from Stream' resolves a new page. The window scope holds a reference for disposal, so the page, its MediaElement and its handlers are never collected while the window lives. DisposeAsync only runs at app or window teardown.

Changing `static readonly HttpClient` to a per-instance field fixes the shared client being disposed by one MediaManager. But every MediaElement now gets its own HttpClient and handler (its own connection pool), when the root-cause fix is to keep the static client and remove `client.Dispose()`. In MediaElement CollectionView or Carousel pages, dozens of MediaManagers each create and dispose an HttpClient for artwork fetches. That means repeated TLS handshakes and socket churn (TIME_WAIT buildup) for no benefit.
